rounds.evidence_text: In a chilling turn of events, Rose is found lifeless in a car, killed by a vial of acid, leading Detective Winston to the affluent suspects, Daisy and Dexter.
Detective Winston found himself in the showroom of a car dealership.
He was eyeing one of the employees behind the counter, a man named Dexter.
The guy was tall, slender, and had a bright grin, almost always painted across his face.
Dexter was seen engrossing himself with trinkets that sat on the edge of his desk.
These weren't just ordinary trinkets, many of them were uniquely car-related, including miniature replicas of cars engines and pieces that Dexter had personally worked on with his chemical expertise.
He smiled lightly as he fiddled with them.
As Winston approached him, Dexter looked up, and his eyes momentarily flickered with recognition before he composed his features into a salesman’s grin.
After introducing himself, Winston mentioned Rose and watched for any reactions.
But Dexter's face remained impassive, his salesman smile never wavering.

Instead of just being a mere salesman, Dexter was also the chief mechanic of the dealership, utilizing his extensive background in chemistry to invent more advanced car maintenance techniques using various chemicals.
His clear talent in this area provided him with a unique edge over other car sale businesses.
As his shift ended, Dexter led Winston to his home, speaking eagerly about his run for a local office.
As they entered Dexter’s living room, Winston noticed a big box sitting against one wall.
Piled around it were numerous trinkets, ranging from keychains to pens, from figurines to pocket watches.
When Winston enquired about the assortment, Dexter revealed his routine of adding to the box each time he made a new customer.
To demonstrate, he showed Winston a trinket he had recently added, telling the detective about the customer he met that day.
It was his way of commemorating their interactions.
The home was filled with telling signs of his life.
One thing that caught Winston's eye was a photo album lying open on the coffee table.
It exhibited Dexter with various people, captions scribbled underneath each picture capturing pleasurable memories.
Their conversation eventually shifted to Dexter’s basement, and his workspace was introduced.

Odd for a car salesman but not for an in-house mechanic, his workspace was filled with extensive glassware and chemicals, including several bottles of acid which Dexter often used in his inventive car mechanic works.
He confirmed to Winston about his background in chemistry before becoming a mechanic and eventually a car salesman.
Just as Winston was preparing to leave, Dexter mentioned something that instantly shocked him.
Rose had threatened to expose him.
She had figured out that he had been dishonest about his qualifications.
Hiding his surprise, Winston empathically responded, and Dexter merely smiled, affirming how damaging Rose's threats were to his public image and his ongoing electoral campaign.
With the resonating echo of Dexter’s last words, Winston bid his goodbyes, exiting with suspicious thoughts playing heavily on his mind.
Not only was Dexter's public image important for his election hopes but, as a renowned mechanic, any scandal could also potentially tarnish his reputation within the car dealership.
The detective, Winston, had strong coffee in his hand as he reviewed the case files laid out in front of him.
His current assignment was the murder of Rose, who was found dead in her car by means of an acid attack.
The type of acid was identical to those found in Daisy's performances.
The perpetrator got away, leaving only a vial as evidence.
Rose had frequent parking spots, and her car was often seen in the lot near the locals' favorite music venue.
The night she was killed, she was leaving a concert that was being performed by Daisy, a singer scheduled to perform at the same venue near the parking lot that day.
Rose also notably had a sizable life insurance policy, to which Daisy was added as a beneficiary just a month before the incident.
Daisy was known for her meticulously neat dressing room.
She claimed it came from her aversion to the generally dirty environment the venues offered.
Daisy's music album sales had been falling drastically, attested by the revenue charts Winston was scrutinizing.
Furthermore, due to the cancellation of many events due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Daisy had been unable to collect performance fees.
During the middle of the practice session, Winston visited Daisy, where she was preparing for her next performance.
He noticed different types of acids in small containers labeled and neatly arranged on a side table.
Upon inquiry, Daisy shared how she often incorporated the acids into her performances for dramatic effects.

She jokingly added, "You should see the mess they make sometimes; this place is never clean."

Witnesses from the concert reported seeing Daisy and Rose leaving the venue together after the show.
They appeared to be the only ones in the car.
Daisy didn't hesitate to confirm, "Oh, yes, Rose and I left the venue together.

She was kind enough to offer me a lift, as my own ride bailed out."

As Winston left the venue, his phone buzzed, reminding him of Daisy's recent addition to Rose's sizable life insurance policy just a month ago.
As he drove past the venue, he saw that it was right next to the parking lot where Rose frequented.
With the vial of similar acid on his mind, the pieces were starting to fall into place for Winston.
Despite making some strides, the detective knew that the journey to justice was far from over.
Each new location and piece of information held the potential to be the key to unraveling the mystery behind Rose's death.

rounds.evidence_text: In the piercing silence of a New York night, Dwayne's life was brutally ended by a sickle's blade in his own car, launching Detective Winston into a dangerous game of truth and lies with suspects, Anthony and Max.
As Winston continued his investigation, his next stop was to meet with Max.
Max ran a popular art dealership in town, claiming to deal with artifacts too, and his reputation had charmed many art enthusiasts, including Dwayne.
Upon knocking, the door creaked open.
Winston found himself in a large living space, filled with exquisite pieces of art, including a rather unique sickle, which was oddly intriguing.
"Max?" Winston called out, taking care not to disturb the artifacts around him.

Max returned from another room, a pleased grin on his face, his eyes kindling with pride," Ah, detective, welcome to my humble abode."

Max was a known art dealer who wasn't just after profit but cherished the art of curating a meaningful collection.
From Winston's observation, Max appeared to be highly concerned about his reputation in this field.
When Winston asked, "Did Dwayne visit you last night?”, from the corner of his eye he noticed a flicker of unease cross Max’s face.
Max hesitated before answering, "Yes, Detective.
He wanted to take a look at my collection...

he had a soft spot for historical farming artifacts."

As they chatted, Max admitted to giving Dwayne a ride afterward as Dwayne was his guest, and thought it only right to drive him back.
Dwayne was seated in the passenger's seat of Max's car, he had said.
It was in this same car where Dwayne's lifeless body was found later.
"So it was just the two of you going to the car?", Winston clarified, to which Max nodded, confirming that he was last seen with Dwayne heading towards the car.
As the discussion continued, Winston learnt from Max about an upcoming exhibit, where Dwayne planned to expose an inauthentic artifact in Max's collection, something that threatened Max’s reputation.
On leaving, Winston couldn't help but echo the words of an old mentor.
In a world where reputation is synonymous with one's identity, public humiliation would surely be a blow to anyone's individuality.
With that he exited, leaving a rather perturbed Max behind him, contemplating the implications.
Winston found himself standing in the midst of Anthony's gallery.
The room was a silent symphony of colors and emotions, none of which were gold.
But gold was the color he was concerning himself with today.
Anthony's housekeeper had testified that she found gold paint on his clothes after his various trips, an unusual finding considering none of his displayed art contained any hint of the metallic hue.
He stepped out to speak with the gallery owner, his heavy boots echoing slightly in the hushed rooms.
"He uses gold paint?" Winston asked, waving a test report he had from Anthony's housekeeper.
"No, not ever in his career.
Anthony's palette is more primary," the gallery owner stated, looking rather puzzled.
After a short nod, Winston tucked away the paper, and left the gallery.
His next stop in the long journey would be to confront Anthony himself.
Anthony had earlier on requested a meeting with Dwayne.
He decided to use this unusual request as leverage, he agreed now to meet Winston by Dwayne's car, a location he knew well since he had keys to it.
He pulled out his phone to arrange this unusual meeting.
Anthony looked a bit out of place amongst the urban landscape, amongst the shining cars.
His hair was a wild mane and colors smudged his skin artistically.
A keychain, bulky and jingling with keys, sat by his side.
"I had to pick up some of Dwayne's things", Anthony said, hand unconsciously stroking the keychain.

"His woman couldn’t do it, she's a wreck."

"You had keys to his car?" Winston prompted.
"Well, yes, we were friends after all," Anthony replied, confirming his synaptic tie to Dwayne's automobile.
Winston decided to take a different approach for the kind of question that lay heavy on his mind.
"Dwayne didn't share your religious beliefs, did he?" He said, more of a statement than a question.
Anthony's face twisted, his features hardened.
"No, he didn't, the fool was way off the path.
He never got my art, my sermons.

I've often stated in my preachings that the nonbelievers like him were threatening the sanctity of our path."

Anthony looked uncomfortable when he realized what he had just said, and he tried to compose himself.
"He needed help, that’s why I wanted to meet him.

Sure, I was deeply offended by his criticism, but that doesn't make my concern any less valid."

"To convince him about your beliefs?" Winston posed, a touch of humanity in his tone.
"No, to make him understand my art!" Anthony's voice was emphatic.
But he didn’t admit to painting with gold.
"There were disagreements then?" Winston asked, almost rhetorically.
A deep sigh rasped out from Anthony's mouth.
"Yes, often.

Unfortunately, I was unable to win him over."

He looked down at his hands, the same hands that relentlessly splashed beautiful, and often disturbing, illusions onto canvas.
And then a grim realization reflected on his face, a bitter parting comment reminding him of the deep offense Dwayne’s criticism might have caused.
The open space around Dwayne's car echoed with the ringing silence-the paradoxical sound of an artist remorseful.
"Ah, it doesn’t matter now." Anthony got up to leave, a sad brush of reality tinted his voice.
The man was an artist, devoted to his spiritual path to the point of obsession.
But enough to commit a murder?
Winston wondered, the many pieces of this puzzle yet to find their right place.

rounds.evidence_text: In the tranquil sphere of the temple, Charlotte's demise by barbed wire disrupts the serenity, drawing Detective Winston into a puzzling web woven by suspects Priscilla and Xenia.
Winston unfolded the clipped newspaper announcement of Charlotte's upcoming wedding.
He scanned the quaint details, turning each over in his mind.
The setting was a temple, a peculiar choice within their community.
Unique also, was the choice of Xenia as the wedding planner.
A woman known for her fastidiousness and deft hands in crafting seamless events.

In a recent chat with Charlotte before her wedding, she mentioned a peculiar detail regarding a certain secret she was advised by Xenia to keep hidden - her past relationship with Xenia's current partner.
It was a secret she was planning to unveil at the altar, a revelation that would surely raise a few eyebrows, with Xenia no longer being the lone keeper of it.
"Ms.
Xenia, I presume?" Winston asked, entering the wedding planner's office.
"Yes.
How can I aid you detective?" Xenia responded, with a slight surprise in her eyes.
"I wanted to talk about Charlotte's wedding...
a ceremony that was slated to occur at the exact minute of her murder.
Noticed anything unusual around those days?” Winston queried.
Xenia hesitated, her expression wavering.
It was clear that the jab about Charlotte's intention to confess the past, which involved Xenia's significant other, had struck a nerve.
The anger simmering in Xenia's eyes was volatile and intense, enough to make anyone uncomfortable.
As they conversed, Winston's attention drifted to an office closet, slightly ajar.
A suitcase peeked from within, stuffed with neatly folded clothes, almost as though it was constantly ready for a trip.
His colleagues had often mentioned seeing this suitcase during their routine meetings with Xenia.
"Ever much of a traveler, Xenia?" Winston asked casually.
She seemed taken aback by his question.
"Sometimes...
it's part of the job.
Last minute trips for a desired decoration, or perhaps to get a gift.

Weekend trips and all."

"That your suitcase in the closet, always packed and ready?" Winston nodded towards it.
Xenia followed his gaze toward the suitcase, then back at him.

"Yes, why?" 

"No reason," Winston shrugged.

"It’s just that colleagues have mentioned spotting you with your luggage at the airport, and at the train station buying tickets – during work hours."

"Yeah, like I said, travelling becomes part of the job sometimes,” countered Xenia, smoothly.

Throughout their conversation about wedding preparations, Xenia specified that she was responsible for every minute detail – setting up and breaking down the décor, liaising with the temple people, overseeing every aspect of the event.
She emphasized that her duties required her presence before, during, and after the ceremony.
Winston mentally jotted this down, noticing how neatly these timings coincided with those of Charlotte's unfortunate fate.

Winston rose to depart, conveying his gratitude, "Thanks for your time."

"Of course, anything to help," Xenia replied softly.
“Charlotte's passing is shocking, but remember, we rely on trust and reputation in our business.
It's all we have.

Charlotte's confession could have marred that."

Detective Winston sifted through the papers littering his desk.
Crime scene photos mixed with witness statements and information on both the victim, Charlotte, and the potential suspect, Priscilla.
Winston ran a hand through his hair, taking a deep breath.
Eyewitness accounts placed Priscilla at the temple on the day of the crime.
The same temple where Charlotte was found, her life taken by barbed wire.
Winston's gaze drifted towards some photos of the hiking trails Priscilla was known to frequent.
The trails, all too often, wound their way past the same temple where Charlotte met her end.
Pushing the papers around, Winston found a report from the local police.
Priscilla's involvement with certain gang activities was far from a well-kept secret.
The faded gang tattoos on Priscilla's skin were testament to her affiliation.
Charlotte, on the other hand, was part of a rival gang, a fact anyone could see from the tags she left behind.
Photos from the trails Priscilla often hiked showed a significant amount of barbed wire fencing.
Winston mused, barbed wire was indeed common along these trails - so much so that Priscilla had even learned to utilize items like it in her own survival knowledge on these hiking expeditions.
A picture of Priscilla hiking caught Winston's attention.
He noted the pair of wire snips she carried.
Those would be potentially useful in dealing with the surplus of barbed wire on her usual trails.
He also noted the rough timeline on the police report.
Charlotte's time of death matched up too neatly with the time witnesses had spotted Priscilla at the temple that day.
"Interesting, isn't it?" Winston muttered to himself, mulling over the facts at hand.
Pushing his chair back, he decided it was time to ask Priscilla some questions.
He was determined to learn the truth, one piece of evidence at a time.

rounds.evidence_text: In a chilling turn of events, Rose is found lifeless in a car, killed by a vial of acid, leading Detective Winston to the affluent suspects, Daisy and Dexter.
Winston was going over the facts of the case when he decided to visit the suspect, Daisy.
Daisy wasn't your typical suspect - she was a singer who always had a passion for her art form, a passion that stood in sharp contrast with her family's dismissive attitude.

“I'm just trying to get ahead in life, you know?" she told Winston as they sat in a small cafe near one of her repeat performance venues - an old building that was frequently harshly criticised for its lack of cleanliness.
"They never cared about my music… always thought it was just a phase.

I couldn't stand their lack of support.”

Getting rid of her family members from her contacts was, as she put it, a "cleansing experience".

It was all very telling of Daisy's meticulous nature - she extended the same cleanliness philosophy to everything in her personal life, hygiene being her top priority; it gave a stark contrast to the venues in which she performed.
After a moment of silence, she casually added, "Sometimes my sarcasm gets the best of me.
I can't tell you how many family dinners I've ruined with it.

My sarcasm stings so hard, it often leaves them in tears."

Winston thought about Rose, who often parked her car in the same vicinity.
"You were scheduled to perform at a place near that parking lot that day… right?" he asked.
Daisy affirmed the fact and mentioned having seen Rose's car, acknowledging that she and Rose were the last two people in the vehicle after her show that night.
As part of her performances, Daisy often integrated different kinds of acid into her routines - the same kind, as it turned out, that had been used to murder Rose.
A cold chill ran down Winston’s spine as he mentally cross-checked the evidence list.
“Acid isn’t a typical instrument for a singer, Daisy..." Winston quizzed, trying to keep the conversation casual.
Daisy just shrugged, "Got to create a spectacle, right?

Attract an audience?”

Daisy had always been adamant about not attending any family gatherings - a fact that did not change even after Rose’s death.
But she claimed to hold no ill-will towards Rose.
As Winston got up from the table to leave, he turned one final time to look at Daisy who was now alone and engrossed in her phone.
A suspect or not, one thing was certain, the story was far from over.
Winston reeked of grease and sweat as he strolled into the electronics store, blinking against the twisted glare of neon and the sharp gleam of fluorescent lights.
Dexter, a wiry man in neatly pressed slacks and a polo, paused in checking and restocking the freshly stocked batteries to greet him.
"You look lost, sir," he called, a spark in his eyes belying the monotony in his voice.
"Actually, I have a few questions for you, if that's not too much trouble," Winston started, flipping open his notepad to gather his thoughts.

A flicker of unease crossed Dexter’s face, but he masked it quickly, "Sure, always happy to help."

Winston dove straight in, "Know a woman by the name of Rose?"

Dexter's face tightened imperceptibly.
"Rose, yeah.
I know of her.
She left her car here to get cleaned the other day.

She told me that she had found an embarrassing picture of me somewhere."

"So, you work on cars too?"

"I...
not exactly.
I was on duty when she came by.
We don't usually offer those services, but I took care of it," he replied, his gaze straying to the poster advertising their recently received new stock of batteries.
"What type of cleaning, exactly?" Winston asked, silently noting another stain on the pristine floors.
just vacuuming, mostly.
People leave all kinds of things in their cars," he concluded, avoiding Winston's steely gaze.

"I found the embarrassing photo of myself in there, the one she had claimed to have found earlier."

"Must have seen a lot of interesting things."

"Yeah, you could say that." Dexter's voice wavered, a hint of bitterness creeping in.

"Were you alone while cleaning the car?"

"Yes.
What's this about?" Panic fluttered in Dexter's eyes just as Winston showed him the same embarrassing photo of Dexter that was making the rounds in town - the one Rose had found.
"Oh," Dexter spoke, all hints of his usual smug demeanor nowhere in sight.
"That...
was circulating at the town gathering...

and Rose had grabbed it and laughed at me as she shown it all around."

"Right," Winston said, making a mental note as he slipped the photo back into the folder.
The laughter, Rose's cruel laughter at Dexter during that town gathering, rang in his memory.

Dexter spoke after a pause, "I...didn't know she still had that."

"One more question," Winston started, leaving the silence to hang as Dexter looked about to collapse.
"Your education...you studied Chemistry?

Specialization, was it industrial acids?"

"Different types, yes," Dexter confirmed, struggling to keep composure.
"Hydrochloric, Sulfuric, Nitric...so many..." His voice trailed off into a whisper as Winston closed his notepad.
"Interesting," Winston remarked, and headed for the door.
The fluorescent store lights flickered as he strode out into the evening, leaving a bewildered Dexter behind in the now-quiet electronics store.

rounds.evidence_text: When the grisly sight of Hugo's lifeless body, axed to death at a campground, meets Detective Winston's eyes, he finds himself entangled in an unnerving hunt for the truth between two suspects - Salvador and Wade.
Winston peered through the misty early morning fog, observing the tranquility of the campground.
He turned to his notes, frowning at the array of facts before him.
This case, the murder of Hugo, was a complicated enigma, and the foggy morning mirrored his confusion impeccably.
He walked over to the climbing area, his eyes locked on the silhouette of a singular climber.
As the figure came closer, the face of Wade, a seasoned mountain climber, surfaced.

He always found the man alert, his axe ready and maintained an aura of determined conviction around him.
"You're out here pretty early.
The mountains talk to you, don't they?" Winston asked casually, glancing over Wade's equipment.
"Yeah, they do," Wade responded, tapping the handle of his axe.
Winston recalled noticing how commanding the axes looked, how Wade always insisted on carrying them on his adventures, whether it was a nearby cliff or a daunting mountain range.
The axes served an instrumental role in climbing, but there was a hidden threat about them.
As the conversation shifted, Winston subtly inquired about Wade’s sister.
It was common knowledge in the campground circles that Hugo had a lecherous eye for her.
The previous day, Hugo was seen lurking ominously near Wade’s sister, arousing fear in her.
It was quite apparent from her pale face after each encounter with Hugo.
Wade was made aware of this predatory stalking by his sister herself.
"Wade, did you and your sister camp here recently?" Winston questioned, briefly scanning the terrain.
Wade nodded affirmatively, a slight twitch in his eye was visible as he rubbed his hand over the polished surface of his axe.
He mentioned they were at the campground on the day of the ghastly murder.
Hugo was present there too, a fact that Winston verified in the campground log.
This piece of information provided a jolt to Winston but he kept it to himself.

As Winston walked away, he turned back for one final look, noticing the tent Wade pointed at; it was a confirmation that they had been camping in the same vicinity as Hugo when the dreadful event transpired.
With the last image of Wade practicing strikes with his axe at an imaginary opponent vivid in his mind, Winston got into his car.
The trail of facts filled his head, developing a labyrinth he planned to navigate, determined to reveal the truth behind this horrific crime.
Winston ran his fingers over the cold side of his coffee mug, his eyes unfocused, drifting towards the crime scene photos splayed across his desk.
Hugo's lifeless body was sprawled in a campground, an axe driven into his chest.
The crime had a brutality that begged attention, even from a detective like Winston who had seen more than his fair share of brutal scenes.
His mind was stuck on Salvador, his primary person of interest.
Salvador was unlike most of Winston's prior persons of interest, in part due to his unique claim that he suffered from a rare medical condition which reacted adversely with moonlight.
While it sounded outlandish to Winston, he did find it odd that Salvador never scheduled any of his driving classes on full moon nights.
When pressed on the subject, Salvador quickly deflected, preferring instead to brag about his latest batch of freshly chopped firewood.
"Lot of freshly chopped wood," Winston mused out loud, glancing at a photograph taken of Salvador's backyard, a handaxe casually leaning against the house.
As a driving instructor, it seemed more than a little odd to Winston that Salvador dedicated so much time to wood chopping.
But Salvador was versatile that way; jumping from being a driving teacher by the day to a lumberjack by evening, all the while feeding a drug addiction that had been spiraling out of control.
Hugo, Winston recalled from earlier investigations, had been Salvador's drug supplier.
He had mentioned to more than one associate that he was thinking about cutting Salvador off, tired of the mounting debt that Salvador was accumulating.
Putting his coffee mug aside, Winston picked up his phone, dialing the local driving institution's office.
"I need to know the names of Salvador's students," he began, leaning back in his chair.
The receptionist at the other end of the line was hesitant, but eventually complied.
"Salvador is really good at what he does," she declared.

"It just that students complain about not being able to schedule classes during full moon nights and he always deflects questions about it."

"Interesting," Winston said, noting her words down.
The mention of Salvador's moonlight 'allergy' triggered Winston's memory of a piece of evidence in Salvador's house - a unique collection of handaxes.
One of those axes could easily be the murder weapon.
Finishing his call and putting down his notepad, Winston sat back, his gaze returning to the photographs of Hugo's grimly lit face.
The pieces were slowly falling in place.
But he knew he was still far from the complete picture.

rounds.evidence_text: In the aftermath of a devastating home explosion that claims the life of Angela, seasoned Detective Winston hones in on two prime suspects: Patrick and Alvin.
Detective Winston grimly regarded the charred remains of Angela's home, considering the pieces of evidence.
Home explosions were not commonly dealt with in his line of work, though he knew very well that such explosives were often used in demolitions.

With such knowledge, he was reminded of a local surfing instructor who also took part in an unconventional part-time job that would put him in frequent touch with explosives, training weekly on handling and disposal.
This wasn't his usual surfing job but his part-time work as a demolition worker.
This was no doubt, Patrick.
Finding his interview notes with Patrick, Winston decided it was time to speak with him again.
Winston had known Patrick through his work, not because he surfed but because of his other role in demolition, an occupation that naturally involved a great deal of work with explosives.
Winston set off to the beach in search of Patrick, eventually spotting him as he was patiently teaching a young boy how to ride the waves.
"Patrick!" he called out to him.
Recognizing Winston, the man navigated back to shore on his surfboard with a practised ease.
"Detective Winston," he greeted, wiping the saltwater off his face.

"How can I help you?"

"Just a few questions," Winston replied.
He opened his notebook to a page of carefully penned notes about Patrick's financial troubles.
"I heard that you've been having some trouble...

getting into a failed investment, left with a sizeable debt?”

Patrick's face tightened, but he nodded in admission.
"That's right.

Lost all my savings, even borrowed a huge amount from Angela, but the investment went under."  

"Angela had been lending you money, huh?" Winston asked, wanting to confirm the loan from Angela.

"And you haven't been able to pay her back because you lost your main job?"

“That’s correct, detective,” the man answered, his face grim with the weight of his troubles.
"Angela ever threaten to, oh, say, call the police on you?" Winston casually asked, inspecting the worn strap of his watch.
Patrick hesitated before finally sighing and admitting, "Yes, she did.
More than once.

I guess she had enough of my money problems and empty promises."

Somewhat satisfied, Winston took down the latest confession.

Glancing around the beach, he then asked, "You were around Angela's house the evening of the explosion?" 

"Detective...
it's not far from here, I often pass by when I go home," Patrick replied, his face tense at the questioning.

"Well, nobody else was around her place at that time," Winston mentioned, "Just an interesting fact."

In the awkward silence that followed, Winston then asked about the part that bothered him the most.

"You use explosives much with your part-time work and your frequent training, Patrick?" 

Patrick seemed to straighten, “I have, yes, in controlled environments and with appropriate permits.” His voice was firm, perhaps a little defensive.
"Right, part of the job, I guess," Winston nodded, closing his notebook.
Not another word was spoken between them as he walked away, leaving a nervous Patrick behind.
Winston gave a slow pull from his coffee as he sat across from Alvin, the typically even-tempered delivery man whose vehicle was loaded and ready for his daily route through town.
Alvin's calm demeanor had earned him a reputation among the townsfolk as reliable, if not a tad peculiar due to his habit of having his lunch beside graves.
Alvin's reliable routine encompassed the entire town including the cemetery - on today's agenda, he'd be stopping at Angela's to drop off a package.
His daily routines had put him on a first-name basis with Angela, as she always made a point to personally welcome him into her home when he arrived with her deliveries.
"So Alvin, any big plans for today?" Winston asked, making casual conversation.
"Oh yes," Alvin replied, a spark in his usually placid eyes.
"I've just bought a vintage Victorian-era coffin from an auction.
Also, I am picking up some decommissioned explosives from a contact in the military.
They're for a historical display I'm working on.

Can't wait to get both set up in the living room."

This interest didn't surprise Winston.
Alvin was known to frequent antique shops, specifically those that boasted a range of mortuary relics.
It was odd, sure, but Alvin being odd was one of the few things that gave him character.
"Did you know Angela?" he asked Alvin in a low tone, a hint of suspicion in his voice.
Alvin nodded, "Yes.
I deliver her packages regularly.

Also," he said after a pause, "I was due to deliver a package to her today."

That tidbit of information Winston knew.
Angela was home that day to get her package, but she had not been prepared for what the delivery contained.
The investigation revealed that the fatal box delivered to Angela's house was filled with explosives, and the only man who Winston knew had any experience with such devices was Alvin.
Alvin’s past in the military gave him the exposure and knowledge about explosives that most people didn't have.
It was common knowledge in their tight-knit community where personal histories were difficult to conceal.
While this knowledge alone didn’t constitute evidence, it was certainly one fact of many that were swirling around in Winston’s head.
As Alvin got up to leave, Winston gave him a tight smile, "I hope you enjoy setting up your new coffin and your explosives display, Alvin," he said.
“Thank you,” Alvin replied, oblivious to any undercurrent in the conversation, his calm demeanor never wavering.
Winston finished his coffee, his mind firmly focused on the explosion that had taken Angela's life, the package that had been delivered, and questions that were begging to be answered.

rounds.evidence_text: In the midst of the arid desert, Jerry's life was brutally extinguished with a lead pipe, and now, it's up to the astute Detective Winston to sift through the sands of deception woven by suspects Maurice and Rex.

rounds.evidence_text: In a shocking twist of events, Charlotte is found lifeless in her kitchen, felled by a stun gun, and it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to unravel the mystery, with prime suspects being Letti and Deborah.

rounds.evidence_text: In the haunting echoes of a cinema hall, Tracy's life was abruptly silenced by the grim stroke of a meat cleaver, leaving Detective Winston grappling with a chilling mystery and two elusive suspects - Nicole and Gloria.

The concert that the Butchers were supposed to play after the movie was now going to be remembered for all the wrong reasons.

One of them catching his eye; a meat cleaver.

Delivering comprehensive experiences is the goal.
Every specification matters, including the banquet," Nicole imparted.
"My past as a culinary student till being a wedding planner helped shape that.

I even received professional training in meat preparation."

"Rumor has it that you made a considerable blunder at Tracy's wedding," Winston broached.

No one is perfect, detective.
However, Tracy blew it out of proportion," Nicole responded, her face growing somber.

For someone like Nicole whose entire business relied on her successful track record as a wedding planner, it could be a fateful blow.
Before confronting her head-on, he decided to examine the perspectives of the eyewitnesses and the CCTV footage.
His eyes strayed to the cold, gleaming steel of the meat cleaver amidst Nicole's kitchen equipment.

rounds.evidence_text: In the quiet tranquility of the city park, Bria's life was abruptly ended with a hatchet, leaving Detective Winston with two prime suspects - Serenity and Naomi.
Winston never loved parks, even when he was a kid.
But nevertheless he walked through the city park, talking with some locals there on their morning strolls.
He was investigating the death of a young woman, Bria, found dead—yes, here—in these park grounds days before.
His steps took him to the park’s community center, a hub that also served as a point of supply for the various camps around the city.
The center stored tools such as hatchets for outdoor activities, usually deployed during camping.
He made his way to the office of Naomi, an intern there working specifically with these tools.
Naomi taught camping skills not only at the center but also at the camps.
She taught how to swing a hatchet, how to build a fire, and overall, how to survive in the wilderness.
Winston knocked, and Naomi opened the door.
Winston noticed bandages on her hands.

“Hello, Naomi,” Winston said, “I understand that you knew Bria?”

“Yes,” she said, “We knew each other.

She… she was very violent towards me.”

“Violent how?”

“She, uhm… she assaulted me.
Several times.
I reported her violent behavior multiple times to the police.
I was even granted a restraining order against her...

at least I had…”

The words hung in the air.
“I was even hospitalized once because of her.

All the time, I felt jeopardized by her continuous attacks” 

“And Bria, she was here the day she was murdered?”

“I was told she was planning to be here that day, yes.
On the same day, I was leading an outdoor skills class.

And it was indeed a strange coincidence, I was teaching people how to use a hatchet for chopping wood.”

“A coincidence,” Winston repeated, looking at the bandages on Naomi’s hands again.
Then, without a word more, Winston turned and left.
He had more people to talk to, and more questions to ask.
Winston flicked his cigarette lighter close, producing a small gust of smoke.
The case was still in its initial stages, but he had already pieced together some revealing tidbits.
He scrawled on the desk all he knew about a woman named Serenity - the prime suspect.
He'd first heard about her from a group who camped locally.
It was their regular outing spot, they'd told him.
"Serenity is always with us..
always got her hatchet in tow.

Her routine was also centered around these creatures.
Apparently, she frequented the library often, particularly the entomology section.

What added to all this was a piece of evidence that Winston couldn't shake off - a letter from the victim.
It had been addressed to Serenity, with Bria explicitly mentioning her intentions to testify.
The letter revealed Bria's possession of damaging information regarding Serenity's singular, and highly illegal, practices in insect collection and preservation.
As he visited the library for some more information, a clerk had passed him an interesting insight.
"That girl Serenity?
Always in the insect section – with her hatchet, too.

Sharpens it while reading, she does."

Winston returned to his table with his thoughts.
As he flipped through the pages of notes, he came upon a second revelation about Serenity's newfound predicament.
After corroborating with several of Bria's friends, Winston learned that Bria had confided in them about her decision to testify against Serenity.
The information Bria had was extremely serious, which could lead to dire consequences for Serenity.
Strengthening his suspicion was one piece of evidence echoing in his mind – a hatchet, freshly used and confiscated from Serenity that eerily matched the deadly weapon at the crime scene.
Forensic reports confirmed that the blood and ridges of the hatchet were an exact match to the murder weapon at park, tightening his grip on Serenity.
Winston could see the connecting dots, but the fear of jumping to conclusions had his caution wobbling on a thin thread.
The day may have ended, but the case had only just begun.

rounds.evidence_text: In the dense, dank heart of the rainforest, Skylar's life was brutally silenced with a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston to navigate a labyrinth of lies, offered up by the two prime suspects - Albert and Mya.
Detective Winston put down Skylar's phone, there was a series of text messages that stood out to him involving an invitation to a camping trip.
He sat back and scratched his chin thoughtfully as it fell into place with the CCTV footage - Skylar and Mya entering the rainforest alone.
Making a note of this, he remembered another piece of CCTV footage from two days back, showing Mya packing for what seems to be a camping trip.
The footage included one notable item within her gear – a lead pipe, distinct because Mya seemed to pay particular attention to it.
He decided to pay a visit to Mya.

She was in a very good shape, her fitness wasn't in question, that was sure.
As she rested between sets, Winston approached her.

“Excuse my interruption," Winston began, "I’ve read that you’ve completed quite a few hiking and mountain climbing expeditions?”

A look of surprise flashed on her face, She nodded, panting a bit.
“Yes, I’ve been fortunate enough to get around…” she replied.

"I understand there’s been tension in the family recently," Winston strayed towards less comfortable territories.

"Skylar had revealed something personal about you to your family, is that right?"

Skylar had no reason to accuse me.” She visibly wilted, there was an anger in her voice, fueled by embarrassment.

“It’s been a dark chapter in my life.”

Winston nodded, understanding.
He had been briefed about Skylar revealing Mya's secret and how the family had started ostracizing her due to the false accusation.
As Mya picked up her gym bag to leave, Winston noticed her camping gear in the open compartment.
The video registered in his mind.
The roll of duct tape, an aluminum water bottle, a headlamp but the lead pipe was missing.
The same lead pipe that was seen on the CCTV footage when she was packing.
It was a small detail but something that stuck with Winston.

Outside the gym, as Winston leaned against his car, one fact bore heavily on his mind - no other cars had been recorded entering or leaving the rainforest by any of the surveillance teams on the day Skylar had been killed.
This little nugget of fact had been disturbing him the entire day.
Winston's face hardened while he made the drive back to his office.
His mind was whirling; he needed to look at the bigger picture.
He was only making sense of each piece that he was uncovering.
Whatever was happening was complex, and he had a lot of facts to untangle.
Winston strolled past the line of cabs parked near the city center.
He had a destination in mind - the beaten grey vehicle at the end.
The driver, Albert, was in the middle of a losing battle with his customer inflow.
Not that the local populace didn't patronize taxis.
In fact, Skylar was the sweetheart of the city, everyone in town loved her and seemed to prefer her company rather than Albert’s.
“Albert, have some free time for a chat?” Winston asked as he leaned into the cab’s open window.
Albert’s gaze didn’t leave the rear-view mirror, covered with a pile of sunglasses.
“Not like I have a lot of customers waiting, detective,” he grumbled.
"Skylar seemed to be collecting quite a few of your regulars.
You seemed to think she was taking away your livelihood.
Did you know her well?" Winston inquired, ignoring Albert's bitter tone.
Albert's eyebrows furrowed as he fixated on the cab’s ornament-studded dash.
"We met a few times.
I was her cab driver for the day.

Imagine the luck.”

“Skylar requested you to drive her to the rainforest that day, didn’t she?”

Albert gave a quick nod, the beginnings of sweat forming on his forehead.
"Yes, and I took a detour.

Figured it would save time.” 

Winston glanced at the windshield, spotting an almost perpetual darkness, and turned back towards Albert.

"You always drive at night, don't you?"

"Yeah, and?" Albert's defensive demeanor wasn’t hard to miss.
"No reason," Winston mused, shifting to open up his field of vision.
“I find it interesting,” he moved on, "because you have a large collection of shades.

You know, considering your night job and all…" 

Albert laughed, a hollow sound echoing in the cab.

"I don't even know what you mean by light sensitivity, detective.”

With a nod, Winston changed topics, "Did you notice anything strange about Skylar that day?

Anything about her demeanor?"

Albert scratched his cheek nervously, avoiding Winston's gaze.

"She seemed pretty normal to me."

"Have any issues making eye contact, for example?" Winston asked, noticing that he himself hadn’t gotten much eye contact during the discussion.
Albert's laugh returned.
It was hollow, yet somewhat nervous.
“N-never been a fan, detective.

Just a thing.”

"Alright, Albert.
Thanks for your time." Winston straightened up, taking one last look at Albert and the cab before turning away.
As far as anyone knew, nobody else was in the rainforest that day - it was just Albert, Skylar, and a host of unanswered questions.
Winston had quite a lot to ponder over.

rounds.evidence_text: In the remote chill of the mountain cabin, Santiago lay lifeless with the trace of a pistol shot piercing the silence, introducing Detective Winston's daunting task of discerning guilt between Orville and Troy.
Detective Winston rubbed his temples as he went through the fact pattern again.

that was new to him.

He lived on that mountain territory, lush with nature and confirmed stories of hidden treasure.
An idyllic hideaway from the hustle and bustle of the city.
A paradise he wasn't willing to share, especially not willing to sell.
He loved his land and nature more than anything else.
Winston glanced at his notes once more when a name caught his attention - Orville.
Orville, an orthodontist by trade with a penchant for pistols, Winston noted, given the several on display when he paid a visit to the man's office.
Orville was also a known hiker, often found rambling about the mountains touching Santiago's cabin.
Santiago's cabin stood alone, hidden away in the mountains which held a deep fascination for Orville, something that Santiago was fully aware of.
Santiago wasn't oblivious to Orville's intentions to purchase the land either, something he had politely but firmly refused.
Sitting deep in thought, Winston recalled the confirmation he had received of Santiago's solitude that fateful day.

Orville had purchased a pistol a week before Santiago's murder.

Tomorrow, he hoped, would reveal some answers.

you never really forget."

The latter had been seen at a local gun store recently, acquiring a shiny new pistol, the perceptive store owner even mentioned Troy buying ammunition that matched the pistol.
Their conversation ended promptly, as Troy resumed reading his book, and Winston made his way back to contemplate further upon the unfolding mystery.

rounds.evidence_text: In the sprawling vineyards of Napa Valley, where grapes for the finest wines are nurtured, the bitter taste of murder lingers as Detective Winston investigates the acid-killed corpse of wealthy vineyard owner Henry, with only the enigmatic Ruben and Michael as his prime suspects.
Winston adjusted the brim of his hat as he stepped through the automatic door, the smell of fresh flowers overwhelming his senses.
He immediately took notice of the intense atmosphere, the air heavy, the shop's occupants quiet.
Looking around, he saw Ruben, the owner of the florist's shop, immersed in his work—grinding powder in a mortar, measuring volatile liquids with a dropper, and then mixing it all.

Winston nodded, trying not to seem too interested.

Ruben's eyes lit up.
"A bird feather, eh?

Winston didn't respond, simply turned to scan the shop, his eyes falling on a young girl huddled in a corner, eyes red with recent tears.

“That’s my niece.

unpleasantness.

"Inappropriate behavior?" Winston asked, seeking confirmation.
Ruben nodded before sighing deeply.

all wrong.

"I understand," Winston said.

A variety of corrosive chemicals, all meticulously labeled and aligned, surrounded him.
Winston leaned back in the shabby chair, hands folded, and stared unblinkingly across the table.
Under the dismal light sat Michael, an archaeologist infamous for his carefree treatment of dangerous substances at the workspace.

He had been caught multiple times not only irresponsibly handling acid, but also indulging in drug use - specifically heroin.

"The vineyard incident, you were there Michael?

Michael seemed surprised by the question but quickly regained composure.
"Yes, I had invited Henry for a stroll around the secluded part of the vineyard.

"Henry..." Winston whispered.

Henry's lifeless body was discovered soon after their encounter at the vineyard, right in the secluded area where Michael had invited him and where they were known to frequent.
"And you've used acid at work for artifact cleaning, right?

"Yes," Michael replied curtly, with an ironic smile clinging to his face, “Taking it for a stroll from work to home wasn’t the best idea.”

Winston grunted, his gaze shifting to the visible injection marks on the man's arms.

“You’ve been caught using heroin, haven’t you, Michael?”

Michael, almost seeming to read Winston’s thought, confessed, "Yes, heroin is my problem.

"But it wasn't only your problem, was it, Michael?
Henry...

Michael's confidence waivered.
He stuttered, “Yeah...

He was going to tell everyone.”

"On records, you have intense training in handling acid and other substances,” Winston pointed out, “At the vineyard too, nobody saw you leave from the secluded part."

Michael fell silent.
Fear was visible in his eyes.
His hands clenched tightly into fists.

Standing up from the table, Winston concluded, “Looks like that day has cost you a lot, hasn’t it?”

For the first time, Michael's often intoxicated demeanor receded, replaced by a sobering silence.

rounds.evidence_text: In the quiet solitude of a local library, Philip is found shockingly murdered with a barbed wire, leaving Detective Winston with the arduous task of sifting truth from alibis of the two main suspects, Hugo and Maria.
Stepping into the library, a sea of hushed whispers and tiptoeing patrons, detective Winston began his appointment with Hugo.
Navigating his way through the maze of bookshelves and study cubicles, he found the man seated in a corner, engrossed in a tangle of wires and knobs.
Hugo was a sound engineer.

The smorgasbord of tools and wires – even a wild-looking barbed one often used in some peculiar sound gigs-, extending around him served as a testament to his profession and the variety of venues he worked in.
"Mr.
Hugo?" Winston interrupted, his voice barely a notch above a whisper.
Hugo nodded, eyelids still glued to his work.
"I'm detective Winston.
I hope I'm not interrupting," he casually commented, glancing at the array of wiring tangled in the engineer's hands.
He took notice of the barbed wire amongst the mix.
A trace of unease settled in the back of his mind as he recalled the crime scene images: Philip, lifeless in the library-turned-crime scene, surrounded by scattered books and barbed wire.
After a moment, Hugo paused his work and leaned back, engaging the detective.
Hugo mentioned a sound engineering job he was working on at the library at the time of Philip's murder.

His work, he explained, often brought him to quiet, empty venues like this after dark, be it a library, an amphitheater, or something else entirely, each requiring specific types of wires and tools, barbed wire included.
"Bit of an unusual pick, isn't it?" Winston tried to sound nonchalant.
Hugo chuckled, revealing a collection of rare and unusual wires he'd acquired as part of his professional routines.
He casually referred to his atypical collection as an occupational hazard, barbed wire included.
The conversation somehow segued to Hugo's family, particularly his brother.
"He's not the responsible, betting kind," Hugo sighed, mentioning a lost gamble that cost his brother significantly.
"Between you and me," he leaned in to confide, "Philip could be pretty aggressive when it came to his debts.

In fact, he was known to resort to physical violence to get his way, a tendency that worried me always."

Detective Winston couldn't help but ask, "Did you confront him about it?"

"No, but..." Hugo hesitated before confessing a private phone call he overheard between Philip and his brother.
Philip, as per Hugo, had not minced words in expressing his threats.
With his booked time slot over, Hugo readied to leave.
Winston noticed the lights around them were already shutting down.
The library often stayed vacant during Hugo's setup and takedown sessions, he mentioned nonchalantly.
As Winston left the dusky library, he contemplated the quiet bulk of sound equipment Hugo had in tow, wires of all sorts jingling together.
It left a disquiet in his gut that he couldn't quite explain.
But as a detective, he was trained to never jump to conclusions.
After all, in a murder investigation, everything and everyone was a piece in the puzzle until proven otherwise.
As Winston walked into Maria's salon, he was overrun by the smell of hair products and freshly brewed coffee.
The salon itself was bustling, filled with happy chatter and the occasional hum of hair dryers.
He was taken in by the sight of Maria, a veteran hairdresser of over 15 years, working diligently on a customer's hair, using an abundance of sharp tools, from scissors to razors.
"Maria?" called Winston.
She looked up, her eyes catching the sheen of the barbed hairpins on her tray.
They looked dangerously sharp - almost eerily similar to barbed wire.
"Yes, that's me!
Can I help you?" Maria responded.
"Just have a few questions," Winston muttered.
Maria's salon, open until 10 pm every evening, was bustling.
As he waited for Maria to finish with her current client, he couldn't help but notice a large unidentifiable bag resting in the corner.
Maria then joined Winston, washing her hands before sitting across from him.
"Detective, isn't it?" she said, having picked up on his official demeanor.
"I often see you at the library," Winston started, hoping his observation could break the ice.
Maria's eyes twinkled as she answered, "Yes, that's true.
I find it soothing to visit the library after I close the salon at 10 pm.

It's open till then, making it a perfect addition to my schedule."

They went on, revealing Maria's deep connection with the library—it came to the point where she became one of its registered trustees and was trusted with its key.
Later, the conversation shifted to her closing activities at the salon.
It didn't take long for Winston to realize the purpose of the large unidentifiable bag.
After closing, Maria would routinely transport this bag to her car trunk, which she conveniently parked just outside.
"I heard from a neighbor that they've seen you cleaning your car in the parking lot after midnight," Winston remarked.
Maria simply nodded, unfazed.
"Yes, I tidy up my car after a long day at the salon.

I usually carry my cleaning supplies in there—it's easier to keep things clean on the go."

The conversation then took a darker turn.
Winston disclosed the tragic news of Philip's demise—he had been found murdered in the library.
His time of death coincidentally coincided with Maria's usual visits.
The revelation hung heavy in the air, but Winston, true to his role, kept his thoughts in check.
His job was to collect information.
Deductions were left to the reader.
After expressing his gratitude to Maria, Winston has left her to continue her work.
Retreating to his car, he began considering his next line of inquiry, Philip's murder fresh on his mind.

rounds.evidence_text: In the glitz and glamour of a bustling casino, a deadly secret unfolds as Iris is found lifeless by a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston with two puzzling suspects - Madison and Christine.
Winston stepped out of the casino, photos of the murder scene clutched in one hand.
Iris' case was looking to be anything but simple.
The security footage he was able to secure put Christine right at ground zero; casino floor, the same night Iris' winning streak took a deadly turn.
He slid into his car, the sound of traffic dulled as his mind replayed the chilling footage.
Christine and Iris, always cooperating so well on their work projects, appeared just as comfortable sharing space in the casino that night.
Sliding the photographs into the evidence bag, Winston started the car.
His first destination for the day; Christine's construction site.
The sound of heavy machinery, power tools and manual labor filled the air as Winston approached the site.
Gazing around the active scene with a professional eye, he watched Christine effortlessly hoist cement bags onto a forklift.
Her muscles rippled from the demanding physical labor of her job, a testament to her dedication.

"Christine," Winston called, catching her attention, "mind sparing a moment?"

Christine nonchalantly wiped sweat from her brow and nodded, making her way over to him.
"Working hard or hardly working?" Winston couldn't resist, despite the grave context of their conversation.
Christine managed to roll her eyes and chuckle.
"I swear, with jobs like these, most men don't even last a day," she casually put.
"It's a wonder how they're even lasting in relationships.
Even people like Peter, Mark, Luke, John, and Matthew couldn't keep up with me.

One month in and they all complained I lost interest."

Winston took note, a smile creeping onto his lips, "You've been quite active, Christine.

Managed to juggle five relationships and it's just May."

Christine smirked, "Well, a lady needs some excitement, doesn't she?"

Winston shook his head in amusement, "Let's bring it back to business, Christine."

Their banter aside, Winston's mind was fully trained on the bitter truth - Iris' regular winning streak at the casino, compared to the lead pipe from the construction site, implied a deadly connection.
Several pieces of the puzzle were falling into place, but he would need more to make his case.
He said his goodbyes, leaving behind the clamor of the construction site.
His day was far from over.
There were still questions to be asked, clues to be found, and a murderer to catch.
The drive to his next destination would give him the chance to mull over what he'd so far uncovered.
The tip of the iceberg, probably, but his determined spirit wouldn't allow him to rest until justice was served.
Winston was looking over the contents of his coffee cup when he got the call.
Iris, a court case witness, had been murdered.
The siren of the crime scene was loud and constant, perhaps a metaphor for the nature of the case which was shaping up to be complex and chaotic.
Squinting under the neon lights of the casino, Winston looked for his suspect, Madison.
The lady in question always wore a hard hat and was often seen by him around the building, repairing things.
She was surrounded by a tool-laden van so often that a casual observer might mistake her for the groundskeeper.
She had her roles in the building, fixing things here and there, seemingly always mending mistakes.
Her worn-out van had become a makeshift storage space for building equipment.
Winston couldn't help but notice the glow from a lead pipe resting within the remaining pile.
The pipe surreptitiously nestled between hammer and screwdriver.
Iris' testimony, scheduled to be presented at the court soon, had been against Madison's illegal shenanigans.
Layers of intrigue were folded over the delicate connection: the lawyer had informed Madison about her upcoming ordeal.
Such update from Madison's lawyer would often coincide with the time she saw Iris leaving for her customary Friday night casino visits.
The irony of it burnt brighter than the burgeoning dawn.
Following a trail of circumstantial evidence, Winston discovered that Madison had been threatened with eviction due to her illicit affairs.
The threat had surely hanged like a smog around her, dark and ominous.
“What a twisted mess!” Winston thought as he rubbed shivering hands over weary eyes.
Frequent visits to the casino by Iris could be seen as just a pastime or, to a mind uncertain of the future, as potential avenues for threat mitigation.
Madison's observations of Iris's Friday night gambles could be a coincidence...
or a clear implication of premeditation.
Casino surveillance tapes confirmed the regular presence.
Madison and Iris, both regular features under the glaring camera lights.
The unblinking eye of the casino camera had captured Madison's presence around the vicinity even as the clock chimed Iris's hour of departure from the world.
Winston found himself standing before the courthouse doors, a paper with fresh ink in his hands.
Iris had been there, holding the very same documents, their legality meant to condemn Madison in a court of law.
Casual yet conspicuous, Madison had been seen overhearing the constant chatter of Iris about her late-night casino visits.
Her lawyer's advice combined with the threat of eviction added fuel to the tension...
Winston sighed deeply as he shielded the court documents from the continual rain.
Piecing together the jigsaw puzzle seemed daunting.
Again, his thoughts revolved around Madison under her hard hat.
His next steps unraveling her story had all begun with Iris' murder.
Now it was only an endless chase after blurry silhouettes of half-truths.
Only time would tell how Madison fits into all of this.

rounds.evidence_text: In the heart of a lively soccer field, Ivy succumbs to a fatal poisoned drink, leaving suspects Meredith and Hugo to face the relentless inquiries of Detective Winston.
Winston walked his fingers over the glossy crime scene photos spread out before him.
The soccer field, typically a place of good-hearted competition and family fun, had been turned into a spectacle of horror as Ivy met her untimely end.
The only saving grace was that the game had been called off before the tragedy unfolded.
Ivy was a frequent attendee of these games, often seen happily sipping on a cold drink from the stand.
This time, it had been her undoing.
Winston was no rookie, but cases like these sent a cold shiver up his spine.
Putting the photos back into the case file, it was time to pay Hugo a visit.
Hugo was perched on a stool in the recording booth when Winston arrived.
Despite the match being called off, Hugo had been working as a sound engineer at the same match.
His work as a sound engineer was only a few blocks away from the matchplex, it was a stone throw away.
Working with sound engineering also meant that Hugo had to handle chemicals regularly as part of his job role.
Winston noticed a tattoo peeking from the arms of Hugo's rolled-up flannel – the name Anna, inked with what seemed like a real sense of devotion.
"Hugo?" Winston asked, leaning against the doorframe.
"That's me," Hugo replied, his eyes never leaving the windows of his booth.
"I hear you were serving refreshments at the match yesterday," Winston said, trying to keep his tone neutral.

"I was, yeah," Hugo confirmed with a nod, "I often help out there."

"You've been seen leaving work that day, "Winston continued.
"Yeah, I left to go set up the refreshments," Hugo responded.
At first glance, Hugo didn’t seem like the type who would care about a toxicology course, but records indicated he had taken one in the past.
Moreover, his work required him to handle complex sound equipment which could involve frequent contact with certain chemicals.
Winston circled back to Hugo's protective side.

"You seem close to Anna."

"Yeah," Hugo’s gaze softened, "hee, she's like my baby sister.

I've always looked out for her."

Any detective worth his salt knew how protective bonds could drive people to extreme lengths.
Winston had heard from others about some cruel remarks Ivy made about ruining Anna and of threats to press charges against her.

"All right Hugo," Winston said, throwing his coat over his arm, "thank you for your time."

Winston had more pieces to the puzzle now, but he knew the killer wouldn't reveal himself easily.
Winston, as always, would be waiting patiently.
After all, a game of cat and mouse was half the thrill of his job.
Winston's latest case had piqued his curiosity, leading him to a popular coffee shop downtown where Ivy, the person of interest, was a regular.
As he strolled in, the distinct aroma of dark roasted beans permeated the air.
Behind the counter, Meredith worked with great efficiency amidst the morning rush.
"Ivy was a regular here?" Winston questioned and Meredith nodded.
"Every morning, like clockwork.
Black coffee, a splash of half-and-half.
No sugar,” she described Ivy's drink preference.
From a nearby television, a clip replayed on the local news – Ivy, laughing boisterously whilst imitating some sacred rituals, unmistakenly disrespecting Meredith's beliefs.

Winston looked towards Meredith, who now busied herself with a new order – an infusion of a variety of substances readily on hand: chocolate shavings, cinnamon sprinkles, and an endless assortment of flavored syrups.
"Do you mix all the drinks?" Winston asked.
Meredith, too preoccupied, responded with a nod.
Every shift, Winston noted, Meredith would arrive donning religious symbols around her neck.
Today was no exception.
As she prepared for her work day, her fingers grazed her amulets and she muttered a silent prayer before diving into the morning pandemonium.

Meredith often spoke publicly about being a staunch follower of her religion and openly declared – more times than Winston would care to count – that anyone who disrespects her beliefs deserves severe punishment.
Right when the morning rush started to wear off, Meredith slipped into the backroom, tugging off her apron.
Winston’s eyes landed on a bag near the entrance - a familiar logo from the local butcher shop from where she regularly purchased raw meat.
In the midst of the bustling shop, Winston's attention was drawn to a framed photograph.
Meredith was captured mid-spit, a chicken wing in hand.
"But she only buys raw meat," the butcher's words echoed in his mind, contrary to the image he was witnessing.

He recalled Meredith’s friends' words: "Meredith has never had cooked meat in front of us."

With lunchtime approaching, the crowd began to ebb and Winston found a moment to delve deeper.
In a passing query, he asked, "Heard about the news?

Ivy, laughing at your beliefs - that was caught on camera."

Meredith’s hands clenched a coffee cup so tightly it overflowed.
In her eyes burned recognition and some suppressed pain.
She merely muttered how disrespectful Ivy was.
A customer chimed in, ordering a highly customized drink and Winston’s observation heightened as he watched Meredith expertly mask all traces of the various ingredients she used in the drink.
A craft eerily similar to certain practices of subterfuge.
As Winston reached out to accept his coffee—an all-black with a splash of half and half, he pondered over the peculiar pieces of the jig-saw.
His goodbye was met with a cautionary note from Meredith, "Hey detective, respect every belief you come across...

seems like the world could use more of that, you know?”

As Winston stepped onto the sidewalk, Meredith’s words left him with a chilling twist in his investigation.

rounds.evidence_text: In the lavish surroundings of a luxury restaurant, Renee's life was cut brutally short by barbed wire; now, Detective Winston must unravel the tangled suspects, Claire and Isla.
Detective Winston had already had a long day, sifting through files, fieldwork, and witness narratives, who mostly tended to exaggerate details.
As his long evening unfolded, he was parked outside a well-lit room; light emanating from a window.
This was Claire's room, which her neighbor distinctly mentioned lights up late into the night when Claire is at her computer.
According her neighbor and to her own roommate, Claire is one who never leaves her room whenever she engages in her internet activities, a detail that struck the detective as particularly strange.
Claire, who happened to be a secretary by day and a waitress at a local restaurant by night, had been on Winston's radar since the case was assigned to him.
The restaurant was also coincidentally the murder scene.
As Winston approached her front door, he couldn't help but notice the enclosed garden, embellished with a line of barbed wire for added security.
It was an unusual choice of boundary protection for a garden, but it held a surreal beauty in the moonlight.

"Claire's gardening was a hobby she fancied in her free time," a neighbor once mentioned, adding that she was adept at handling the barbing without ever having an injury, a skill that had surprised many.
In their brief conversation, her roommate had mentioned the elusive yet frequent late-hour typing noises coming from her room and how suddenly they would stop whenever she tried to enter.
"I always found it strange.
She would immediately shut her laptop, and I didn't really see what she was working so late into the night.
It wasn't like her," the roommate remarked.
"All these late-night activities don't necessarily mean any harm," Winston murmured to himself.
As the evening progressed, Winston found out from the restaurant's janitor that there was ongoing construction by the restaurant.
The presence of the surplus barbed wire stockpile meant that it was a common sight in their vicinity.
Renee, the victim, was more to Claire than just an overseer at the restaurant.
Renee, amidst her work, had unexpectedly stumbled upon Claire's illegal embezzlement activities linked to the restaurant's funds.
Word was, she was about to expose these allegations, which would have undoubtedly cost Claire her job and possibly lead to incarceration.
As Winston drove back, battling an oncoming headache, he lit up a cigarette.
The day had been long, crammed with ongoing conversations filled with facts and stories.
As he watched the ember crush under his boot, his instincts whispered that there was a long path ahead before he could find resolution.
Winston sat down at his desk, shuffling through the case files.
The file named 'Renee' seemed to be the one that took his interest.
He pulled out the notes from the coroner's office; Renee had been found some time earlier at the two-Michelin-starred L'etoile Restaurant.
Shrugging on his coat, Winston walked toward the door, picking up the file enroute.
He hailed a cab and slipped the driver an address halfway across town; the scene of the murder - a now-closed luxury restaurant.
Inside, a crowd had made the regular police's work a little more difficult.
Separating potential suspects from huddling, shocked patrons was decidedly hard.
Winston walked up to a uniformed officer and learnt from him that a crowd of people were dining at the restaurant when the crime was committed; among them was a woman named Isla.
A trip to her house later, Winston found himself in front of a woman with an achingly passionate love for her favorite music group.
He couldn't help but notice a collection of survival tools on a nearby rack reflecting the afternoon sunlight.
As he browsed, he found several open tabs on her computer that linked to various tutorials and forums about survival skills.
It was known to him, from a previous informant, that Isla had been learning survival skills through those online sources.
He remembered learning earlier that Isla had defended her home against an intruder with a piece of barbed wire once.
As he was about to leave, he noticed a receipt on the coffee table.
It was from a local hardware store barely a day old and listed 'barbed wire' as one of the items.
Isla showed Winston out of the house, all the while talking passionately about her favorite music group.
They were up for the same award that Renee's group ultimately won.
"It ain't fair, you know?" she complained.

"My boys deserved it, not them."

A canvas of previous police reports showed that she had been in a couple of discrimination lawsuits.
Neighbors had heard her speak poorly of Renee's culture.
Winston made his way back to L'etoile Restaurant.
The manager handed him the reservations book.
Renee had booked a table for the night of her death.
Not far from her entry was another name that seemed all too familiar - Isla.

rounds.evidence_text: In the midst of neon lights and the scent of plastic, Detective Winston finds himself investigating a chilling case: Eugene, bludgeoned to death with a nunchaku in a laser tag arena, with only Timothy and Adam as the potential culprits.
Detective Winston sat quietly at his desk, looking through the folder of the victim Eugene.
Eugene had been a regular player at the local laser tag arena and had just recently spoken publicly about an upcoming event.
Tragically, the last event proved fatal for him.
Winston moved his attention from the depressing case files to a stack of books lent to him by the local library.
All were martial arts manuals.
He grabbed one at random and idly flipped through it.
Being a tenured police officer, he could tell those books had been heavily used.
The slight creases on the spine, the wear on the edges of the book indicated to someone's use.
And that someone happened to be his prime suspect: Timothy, the novelist.
Timothy was known for his meticulous crafting of characters, mimicking their behaviors and mannerisms.
He was currently working on a secretive character.
People often tried to ask about Timothy's childhood to understand better where he derived his characters.
However, he generally kept his past to himself.
Locating Timothy's house, Winston decided it was time to pay a visit.
Winston knocked on the door, and eventually, Timothy answered.
"Detective Winston," Winston said, holding up his badge.

"Do you mind if I ask you a few questions?"

With Timothy's compliance, they settled on the sofa in the living room.
Winston noticed more martial arts books on the coffee table, and the various photos of Timothy at martial arts classes that lined the walls.
"You seem to have a great interest in martial arts," Winston observed.
"Yeah, I go to a class every week," replied Timothy.

"It helps me in my writing."

"Dabbling in martial arts for your new character?" asked Winston curiously.
"Indeed," replied Timothy with a laugh.
Timothy's phone buzzed, disrupting their conversation.
After checking it, he made a face and sighed.
He put it aside, glancing at Winston.

"Let's not dwell on the past, shall we?"

Surprised by Timothy’s response, which he typically gave when people asked about his childhood, Wiston decided to redirect the conversation.
Timothy then pointed to a stack of documents on the coffee table, "I signed up for the laser tag event.
Eugene and I were planning to be on the same team.

We played together all the time."

Remembering Eugene's public announcement and the photos of Timothy at the laser tag events, Winston nodded.
Time to tackle one case at a time.
As Winston left, he got a clearer picture of Timothy: the martial artists manuals, the laser tag documents, and Timothy's habit of immersing himself into his characters.
All this information was creating a mind map of the situation in his mind.
Winston finished his cup of morning joe, reading through the tedious paperwork once more.
Eugene had been found dead in the laser tag arena, laying coldly next to neon walls and the echoes of laughter.
The weapon of choice, a nunchaku, placing a grim shadow over childhood fun.
It seemed the murder had taken place during the team building event itself.
Ready for another day in the field, Winston decided to visit his only suspect, Adam, owner and operator of a local zoo.
He arrived at the zoo just in time to witness the unique spectacle of Adam deftly practicing martial arts with a nunchaku within one of the empty enclosures while the animals were being fed.
Adam was a stout man, seemingly, as comfortable with dangerous animals as he was with the simple tasks of running a zoo.
Each enclosure had a plaque, with a little note, 'Owned and managed by the Jones family for generations'.
Adam was the newest torch-bearer of the Jones family legacy.
"You Adam?" asked Winston, walking towards him.
"Yes, sir.
Is there something you need?" replied Adam, dusting off his hands.
"I'm Detective Winston, looking into the murder of Eugene.

I understand you two were at a team building event together?" 

"We were in the same laser tag team.
Yes, it was hardly a pleasant event, considering how it ended," Adam responded, a thin veil of remorse could be detected in his gaze.
"Witnesses have said that they saw you two chatting during the event - an argument perhaps?" Winston continued.
Adam didn’t deny it.
"We did, over a few allegations he made about my zoo.

He was putting it on the record that there were multiple safety violations here."

Winston changed the subject, "Did you buy something from the gift shop here at your zoo?

Maybe...nunchaku?"

Adam, startled by Winston's directness, simply tipped his cowboy hat in acquiescence.
"Yeah, I bought one from our shop.

I've practiced some martial art forms using nunchaku during my free time, mostly right here at the zoo."

Taking that in, Winston asked further.

"How about your feeding times?"

Adam arched an eyebrow and gestured towards the animals, replying "Usually line up with the martial arts classes at town sports center, why?"

Winston gave a dismissive wave of the hand, "Just curious.

Take care, Adam."

With that, Winston retreated to collect his thoughts.
One thing he knew for certain, the list of suspects wasn't going to extend beyond this zookeeper for a while.
